analysis.one_liner: Requires the President to justify new tariffs to Congress, which must approve them or they expire.
analysis.headline: Referred to two House committees on April 7, 2025, the tariff-review bill has seen no hearings, markups, or votes since, despite 8 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: Tariffs — taxes the President can put on imported goods — are ultimately paid by U.S. importers and passed on to shoppers in higher prices. This bill would require the President to tell Congress within 48 hours after imposing or raising any tariff, explaining why and estimating the impact on U.S. businesses and consumers. Any new or increased tariff would expire after 60 days unless both chambers of Congress pass a law approving it, and Congress could end a tariff sooner with a resolution of disapproval.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that bear tariff costs. Tariffs are paid by the U.S. importer, and studies of past tariffs show much of that cost is passed to consumers through higher prices. By requiring a stated rationale and a consumer-impact estimate, and by making every new tariff die after 60 days unless Congress affirmatively approves it, the bill gives shoppers and import-reliant firms a check on price-increasing tariffs — and gives every member of Congress, not just the President, the power to force a fast vote on whether a tariff should stand.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households and businesses paying tariff-driven prices

how_it_helps.text: The President must notify Congress within 48 hours of imposing or increasing a tariff, including the reasoning and an assessment of the potential impact on U.S. businesses and consumers — creating a public paper trail for price increases, rather than tariffs appearing by announcement alone.

Any new or increased tariff expires after 60 days unless Congress passes a joint resolution of approval signed into law, so no tariff can take effect and stay without a vote by the people's elected representatives.

Any member of either chamber can introduce a resolution of disapproval at any time after the notification, and those resolutions get expedited fast-track procedures (borrowed from the trade-law process normally used for trade agreements), so Congress is not dependent on committee chairmen to force a vote on a tariff.
If a disapproval resolution is enacted, the duty immediately ceases to have force or effect, giving Congress a way to cancel a tariff that is raising prices without waiting for the 60 days to run.

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, the President and the executive branch would give up unilateral control over tariffs, and domestic industries that profit from tariff protection (steel and other shielded producers) would lose that protection whenever Congress declined to approve it. Businesses that use tariffs as negotiating leverage would also lose the ability to keep one in place indefinitely without legislative backing. Consumers, by contrast, would bear less of the tariff burden.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not bar a president from simply imposing the same duty again and again, restarting the 60-day clock each time; a determined administration could keep a tariff functionally alive through repeated re-imposition while formally complying with the review requirement.

A 60-day expiration could blunt tariffs' value as negotiating leverage: trading partners would have an incentive to wait out the clock, and the administration would have to win votes in both chambers to keep pressure on — a real trade-off that honest supporters of the bill must acknowledge.

The bill could slow a genuinely needed emergency tariff response, though it excludes antidumping and countervailing duties (the standard tools against foreign goods sold below cost or subsidized), which limits how much emergency trade-remedy power it actually touches.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: it converts presidential tariffs from a unilateral, indefinite action into something that must be explained, priced out for consumers, and voted on by Congress. The check is softer than it looks, because nothing stops a president from re-imposing the same duty to restart the clock, and the 60-day expiration could weaken tariffs as leverage in trade negotiations. On balance, the transparency and the mandatory vote outweigh the leverage concern, but the bill would not end tariffs — it would subject them to a legislative test.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means and Rules committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee has taken any action on it, so it is waiting with no vote scheduled.

narrative.text: On April 7, 2025, Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) introduced the bill with three original cosponsors from both parties — Reps. Will Hurd (R-CO), Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ), and Gregory Meeks (D-NY).
The Speaker referred it to two committees the same day: Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tariffs, and Rules, which controls how bills reach the floor.
Eight members total have signed on as cosponsors — 3 Republicans and 5 Democrats — making this a bipartisan measure, though a thinly subscribed one relative to the size of either chamber.
Since that referral, the action record shows no hearings, no markups, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has gone nowhere, the President keeps unilateral power to impose or raise tariffs without congressional approval, and tariff-protected industries keep their shield. Consumers and import-reliant businesses get no review or expiration of tariffs. Nobody has formally killed the bill, so a future push remains possible, but as of now the lack of action preserves the status quo.

sides.party_line_note: No chamber has voted on the bill, so there is no roll-call to read; sponsorship is bipartisan, with 3 of 223 House Republicans and 5 of 217 House Democrats signed on.

industries.note: The bill strips the presidency of the power to impose or raise tariffs unilaterally and keep them in place indefinitely; every tariff would need a 48-hour justification and an affirmative vote of Congress to survive past 60 days. Because unconstrained tariff power shows up as higher prices on imported goods for households, the executive's interest in keeping it runs against consumers' interest in this bill.

industries.industry: Tariff-protected domestic industries (steel, aluminum, and other shielded producers)
industries.note: Their tariff protection would lapse after 60 days unless Congress votes to keep it. Protection raises prices for the industries and consumers that buy the protected goods, so their interest here runs against ordinary shoppers.

These firms pay tariffs on materials and goods they bring in and pass much of that cost to their customers. Automatic expiration and a congressional disapproval route give them a way to get price-raising tariffs lifted.

analysis.trajectory: Congress is still in session, so the bill is technically alive, but the pattern is unfavorable: tariff-reapproval measures have repeatedly stalled in this Congress, and Ways and Means — the committee that controls tariff legislation — has shown no sign of scheduling it. Unless the Speaker's office decides the issue deserves floor time or supporters build a discharge petition (a device to pull a bill out of committee over the leadership's objection), it is likely to sit without action until the session ends. Its prospects would improve mainly if tariff-driven price increases become a more central political issue.
